title: Every Bell test that a given extreme quantum correlation maximizes, in the simplest scenario
authors: Yutian Wu, Xie Sicheng, Ravishankar Ramanathan
problem: In the simplest Bell scenario, two parties each choose between two measurements with two outcomes. The quantum correlations they can produce form a convex set \(\mathcal{Q}_{2222}\), and an experiment aiming at device-independent randomness or self-testing usually targets one extreme point of it. Many Bell expressions are maximized at the same extreme point, and they respond differently to detector loss and noise. Which Bell expressions are maximized at a given nonlocal extreme point? The complete answer is the normal cone of the set at that point, which had been worked out only at the Tsirelson point and along one curve.
result: For every nonlocal extreme point the normal cone is constructed explicitly. Bob's four conditional states, one for each input and outcome of Alice, give four tangent Bell expressions. A Bell expression is maximized at the point exactly when it is a nonnegative combination of these four, it is stationary when the angle between Bob's two measurements is varied, and no one of the sixteen local deterministic strategies gives it a larger value. For the family of Wooltorton, Brown and Colbeck the normalized cone is a quadrilateral. As an application, for every detector efficiency between \(0.75\) and \(0.98\), the authors give a two-qubit experiment and a Bell score that certify between about \(9\%\) and \(18\%\) more single-round min-entropy than any CHSH score at the same efficiency.
significance: The result turns a geometric question into a finite recipe: four vectors, one linear equation and sixteen inequalities. That makes it possible to search the whole family of Bell tests with a given ideal behaviour, for example for the one that loses least to detector inefficiency, and to know that nothing in the family has been missed. The detector-loss example shows the freedom is worth having in practice: the score, not only the device, decides how much randomness one observed number can certify.
limitations: The construction relies on the special structure of this scenario, where every extreme point has a two-qubit realization and Bob's conditional states lie on an ellipse; the authors leave larger scenarios open. The randomness comparison is for single-round min-entropy certified from one Bell value, without finite-statistics effects, and it does not claim the chosen scores are optimal or better than certification from the full statistics. The variational formula for quantum bounds (Appendix A) and the full sufficiency proof (Appendix B) were not checked here. The authors state that Grok 4 and GPT-6-Astra assisted in developing the proof of Theorem 1 through iterative discussion, and that they verified all steps.
summary_basis: Description based on the arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-24: Secs. I–V, including the construction (Lemmas 1–2, Eqs. 8–24), the proof sketch of Theorem 1, Box 1, the Wooltorton–Brown–Colbeck family (Sec. III) and the detector-loss application with Table 1 (Sec. IV). Appendices A–D, including the full proof of Theorem 1, were not read. Editorial checks: Box 1 was implemented and applied at the family's maximizers for delta = pi/8, 0.3 and pi/6. The common overlap came out as −sin(delta), the normalized cone was a quadrilateral, and each of its four vertices had quantum maximum 1.000000 at the target, found by optimizing two-qubit Bell operators over all projective measurements. The expression I_delta itself lies inside the cone, and a single tangent expression, which violates stationarity, reaches 1.99, 1.71 and 2.46 instead of 1. At three generic points from partially entangled states the cone sections had 7, 6 and 6 vertices, all with quantum maximum equal to the target value. The improvements in Table 1 recompute to 9.2% at eta = 0.75 and 18.0% at eta = 0.90.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: A behaviour in this scenario is fixed by eight numbers: Alice's two outcome biases \(\alpha_x\), Bob's two biases \(\beta_y\), and four correlators \(E_{xy}\). A Bell expression is a linear function \(\vec g\cdot\vec p\) of these eight numbers. Its quantum bound is the largest value over \(\mathcal{Q}_{2222}\), and it supports the quantum set at \(\vec p\) when \(\vec p\) attains that bound. The supporting expressions at \(\vec p\) form a convex cone, the normal cone. After fixing the value at the target to one, a recent result of Liu, Zingarofalo, Barizien and Bancal shows that this section is at most two-dimensional.

The construction starts from Bob's side. When Alice measures input \(x\) and gets outcome \(a\), Bob's qubit is left in a state whose two expectation values form a point \(\vec w_{a|x}\) in the plane. All such points allowed by Bob's two measurements lie inside an ellipse fixed by the overlap \(c\) of his measurement directions. The authors prove that a nonlocal extreme point determines this overlap uniquely, and that all four points lie on the ellipse's boundary. The tangent line at each boundary point is a linear inequality on Bob's expectations, and multiplying by Alice's outcome probability turns it into a Bell inequality. Those are the four tangent expressions.

Any nonnegative combination of the four tangents is maximized at the target among behaviours with the same overlap \(c_0\). Two more conditions are needed to beat behaviours with other overlaps. Rotating Bob's directions changes the overlap along a smooth curve of quantum behaviours through the target, so a supporting expression must have zero derivative along it. No local deterministic strategy may exceed the target value either. Theorem 1 states that these necessary conditions are also sufficient. The proof sketch uses the determinant of one minus the two-qubit Bell operator as a polynomial in the overlaps, whose leading coefficient has the sign of the product of the four correlator coefficients.

For the one-parameter family \(\mathcal{I}_\delta\) of Wooltorton, Brown and Colbeck, whose maximizers certify two bits of global randomness, the normalized normal cone is a quadrilateral with explicit vertices. The application then models detectors of efficiency \(\eta\) that record \(+1\) when they fail to click. Every recorded score is a fixed affine transformation of a score on the ideal behaviour, so a family of loss-adapted tests is obtained by pulling the normal cone back through that map. Searching this family over two-qubit devices, and certifying the results independently with guessing-probability bounds, gives the comparison with CHSH at 112 efficiencies covering \([0.75,0.98]\).

Table 1 lists six reference points. At \(\eta=0.90\) the selected score certifies at least \(0.198626\) bits per round, while no CHSH score certifies more than \(0.168313\). At \(\eta=0.75\) the figures are \(0.009845\) and \(0.009013\). Between grid points the authors argue by deliberately discarding clicks, which reproduces a lower-efficiency experiment. Code and certificate data are in a public repository. Open questions are finite-statistics selection of scores and comparable constructions beyond two inputs and two outputs.

methods.technique: Tangent Bell expressions from Bob's conditional-state ellipse
methods.explanation: Each of Alice's measurement events prepares a state for Bob, and the expectations of Bob's two observables in that state lie on an ellipse. The tangent line to the ellipse at that point becomes a Bell inequality after multiplying through by the probability of Alice's event.
math: From the eight coordinates, Bob's conditional expectation of \(B_y\) when Alice obtains \(a\) on input \(x\) is \[w_{a|x,y}=\frac{\beta_y+aE_{xy}}{1+a\alpha_x}.\] For a nonlocal behaviour the denominator is positive: if Alice's outcome for some input were certain, a local model would exist. Write \(B_y=\vec n_y\cdot\vec\sigma\) with \(c=\vec n_0\cdot\vec n_1\) and \(G_c\) the \(2\times2\) Gram matrix with ones on the diagonal and \(c\) off it. A Bloch vector \(\vec m\) gives \(\vec w=(\vec m\cdot\vec n_0,\vec m\cdot\vec n_1)\), and \(\vec w^{\mathsf T}G_c^{-1}\vec w\) is the squared length of the projection of \(\vec m\) onto the measurement plane. Hence \[\vec w_{a|x}^{\mathsf T}G_c^{-1}\vec w_{a|x}\le 1.\]

Lemma 1 shows that at an extreme point only one overlap \(c_0\) is consistent with all four constraints. If two overlaps \(c\ne d\) were, write the constraint as \(F_{a|x}(c)\le0\) with \(F_{a|x}(c)=w_0^2+w_1^2+c^2-2cw_0w_1-1\), which is \(1-c^2\) times \(\vec w^{\mathsf T}G_c^{-1}\vec w-1\). The identity \(F(\tfrac{c+d}{2})=\tfrac12[F(c)+F(d)]-\tfrac14(c-d)^2\) would make all four constraints strict at the midpoint, and a small neighbourhood of \(\vec p\) would then be quantum, contradicting extremality. Lemma 2 shows the four points lie on the boundary, because an extreme point has a pure real two-qubit realization in which Bob's conditional states are pure.

At a boundary point the outward normal is \(\vec v_{a|x}=G_{c_0}^{-1}\vec w_{a|x}\), and every allowed \(\vec w\) satisfies \(\vec v_{a|x}\cdot\vec w\le1\). Substituting the expression for \(w_{a|x,y}\) and multiplying by \(1+a\alpha_x\) gives the Bell inequality \[-a\alpha_x+\sum_y v_{a|x,y}\,\beta_y+\sum_y a\,v_{a|x,y}\,E_{xy}\le 1,\] tight at the target. Editorial check: at \(\mathcal{I}_\delta\)'s maximizer, computed numerically, the common root of the four quadratics is \(c_0=-\sin\delta\), the overlap of Bob's two observables in the known realization.
methods.transfer: Whenever a correlation set is the image of a set of conditional states, tangents to the state space at the conditional states give candidate supporting functionals. Steering scenarios and prepare-and-measure tests with a qubit receiver have the same structure.

methods.technique: Stationarity along a measurement rotation, plus sixteen local comparisons
methods.explanation: The tangent combinations beat every behaviour with Bob's overlap fixed at \(c_0\). To beat behaviours at other overlaps, the Bell value must not increase to first order when Bob's measurements rotate. Comparison with the local vertices then rules out the remaining competitors.
math: Keep the shared state and Alice's measurements fixed and rotate Bob's directions in their plane, giving a curve \(\vec p(c)\) of quantum behaviours with \(\vec p(c_0)=\vec p\). If \(\vec g\) is maximized at \(\vec p\), the function \(c\mapsto\vec g\cdot\vec p(c)\) has an interior maximum at \(c_0\), so \[\vec g\cdot\dot{\vec p}=0,\qquad \dot{\vec p}=\frac{d\vec p}{dc}\Big|_{c_0}.\] Local behaviours are quantum, so \(\vec g\cdot\vec d\le\vec g\cdot\vec p\) for the sixteen deterministic vertices \(\vec d\). With \(\vec g=\sum\mu_{a|x}\vec\gamma_{a|x}\), \(\mu\ge0\) and \(\sum\mu=1\), these are one linear equation and sixteen inequalities in four unknowns, so the normalized cone is a polygon.

Sufficiency is the hard direction. In the two-qubit reduction the Bell operator \(H\) depends on Alice's and Bob's overlaps, and \(\Delta=\det(I_4-H)\) is a polynomial of degree at most two in each. The target is a stationary zero of \(\Delta\), and the leading coefficient has the sign of \(\prod_{x,y}g_{E_{xy}}\). When that product is nonpositive, restricting \(\Delta\) to a line gives \(\sigma^2q(\sigma)\) with \(q\) concave, and the local comparisons make it nonnegative at the endpoints, where one party's observables commute. So \(\Delta\ge0\) throughout, which is upgraded to \(I_4-H\succeq0\). When the product is positive, a local model beats the target, which the local comparisons forbid.

Editorial check of the conditions' role: at \(\delta=\pi/6\) the single tangent \(\vec\gamma_{+|0}\) has value one at the target but derivative \(0.577\) along the rotation, and its quantum maximum is \(2.464\). The combination \(\mu=(\tfrac16,\tfrac13,\tfrac16,\tfrac13)\), which is \(\mathcal{I}_{\pi/6}\) normalized, has zero derivative and quantum maximum exactly one. For detector loss, recorded behaviours are \(L_\eta(\vec q)=\Lambda_\eta\vec q+\vec k_\eta\), so \(\vec g\cdot L_\eta(\vec q)=(\Lambda_\eta^{\mathsf T}\vec g)\cdot\vec q+\text{const}\), and the loss-adapted family is \(\{\vec g:\Lambda_\eta^{\mathsf T}\vec g\in N_{\mathcal Q}(\vec q)\}\).
methods.transfer: Necessary conditions from a one-parameter family of realizations plus checks at a finite set of vertices is a general route to supporting hyperplanes of semialgebraic sets. Pulling a normal cone back through an affine noise map is the way to adapt any family of witnesses to a known imperfection.
